blocks.text: Sources of pollution may be small and at a single point, or many locations adding the same or different kinds of pollution. On this basis, sources of water pollution are divided into two types.

blocks.title: Point-source pollution
blocks.text: Point-source pollution is contamination that enters a water body from a single, discrete and identifiable location or point.

Because the discharge is concentrated at one point, it often causes a pollution plume. Just downstream of the discharge, the concentrations of the pollutant (such as heavy metals or organic waste) are highest, causing local acute toxicity. Examples are a factory discharging lead or mercury salts directly into a river through a wastewater pipe, and a storage tank at a chemical plant leaking its contents into the soil and then into the groundwater.

blocks.title: Non-point source (NPS) pollution
blocks.text: Non-point source pollution, also called diffuse pollution, occurs when rainfall or snowmelt moves over and through the ground, picks up natural and human-made pollutants, and finally deposits them into lakes, rivers, wetlands and coastal waters.

Unlike point sources, NPS pollution depends heavily on weather events such as heavy storms. It gives a mixture of pollutants at lower concentrations over a much wider area. Examples are rain washing excess ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3), fertilisers and pesticides from thousands of hectares of farmland into a river system, and stormwater moving over hard surfaces such as roads and car parks, collecting leaked engine oils (hydrocarbons), zinc from tyres and road salts.

blocks.alt: Left, point source: a factory pipe runs into a river and an orange plume spreads downstream from the outlet; examples are a factory releasing lead or mercury salts and a leaking storage tank. Right, non-point source: a rain cloud over three fields and a road, with many arrows carrying runoff into the river along its whole length; examples are NH4NO3, fertilisers and pesticides from farms, and oils, zinc and road salts from roads.
blocks.caption: Point and non-point sources (original diagram for topic 33.2).
blocks.long_description: A point source enters at one identifiable place, so it is concentrated there and easier to control. A non-point source enters along a wide area with runoff after rain, so it is diluted but hard to trace.

items: Classify as point or non-point sources, with reasons: (i) outfall pipes releasing treated sewage from treatment plants into a bay or river; (ii) acid rain from nitrogen oxides from distant traffic or power stations dissolved in rainwater.
Give two major differences between point and non-point sources of pollution.
